html:
The big picture

The lecture finishes collisions and then builds the whole rotational copy of linear dynamics. (1) A block runs into a spring on a rough floor: energy conservation with friction gives the coefficient of sliding friction from the measured compression. (2) Momentum conservation from 12 Energy Conservation in Practice, Momentum and Collisions is applied to a sticking collision in 2D and to recoil (rifle, a person throwing a ball). (3) In an elastic collision momentum and kinetic energy are conserved; the two equations combine into "the relative velocity reverses", which gives the final velocities and their limiting cases. (4) When mass is added or removed continuously (a conveyor belt), \vec F = \mathrm d\vec p/\mathrm dt gets an extra term: a system of variable mass. (5) Rotation gets its own quantities: \vec v = \vec\omega\times\vec r, torque \vec T = \vec r\times\vec F, and the moment of inertia J = \sum m_i r_i'^2, which appears in the rotational kinetic energy E_\text{rot} = \tfrac12 J\omega^2. The integral form gives J of a hollow cylinder, and the parallel-axis theorem (Steiner) moves J to any parallel axis. (6) Every linear quantity has a rotational partner (m\to J, v\to\omega, F\to T); the partner of momentum is angular momentum \vec L = \vec r\times\vec p = J\vec\omega, changed only by torque, \mathrm d\vec L/\mathrm dt = \vec T. Without external torque \vec L is constant (conservation of angular momentum): the skater spins faster with her arms in, and a spinning wheel on a stool shows that \vec L is a vector.

1 Energy with friction: a block runs into a spring

Lecture: p. 1 top · Giancoli §8-6

Pasted figure (two panels): (a) a block m slides with speed v_0 toward a spring k fixed to a wall; (b) the block compresses the spring; on it act the normal force F_N (up), the weight (down), the friction force F_R (to the left, against the motion) and the spring force F_F (to the left). The figure's labels are German: F_R = Reibung (friction), F_F = Feder (spring).

This continues the energy-with-friction problems of 12 Energy Conservation in Practice, Momentum and Collisions › 4 Energy with friction: the ramp. The block arrives at the relaxed spring with kinetic energy \tfrac12 m v_0^2. By the time it stops, at the maximum compression x, that energy has gone two ways: into the spring, \tfrac12 k x^2 (11 Gravitational Field, Work, Kinetic and Potential Energy › 8 Potential energy), and into heat, the friction force times the distance x. The floor is flat, so gravity's potential energy doesn't change and F_N = mg, hence the friction force is \mu_d m g:

\frac12 m\cdot v_0^2 = \frac12 k\cdot x^2 + F_R\cdot x = \frac12 k\cdot x^2 + \mu_d\cdot m\cdot g\cdot x
Symbols
  • m — mass of the block (kg); v_0 — its speed when it touches the spring (m/s)
  • k — spring constant (N/m); x — maximum compression of the spring = distance slid while compressing (m)
  • F_R — sliding friction force (N), always against the motion; the board writes it F_\rho in the first line
  • \mu_d — coefficient of sliding (dynamic) friction, dimensionless; g = 9.81\ \mathrm{m/s^2}

The lecture solves for \mu_d, which turns the experiment into a way to measure friction:

\begin{aligned} \mu_d\, m g x &= \tfrac12 m v_0^2 - \tfrac12 k x^2 && \text{(bring the spring term to the left side)} \\ \mu_d &= \tfrac12 m v_0^2\cdot\frac{1}{m g x} - \tfrac12 k x^2\cdot\frac{1}{m g x} && \text{(divide by } m g x) \\ &= \frac12 v_0^2\cdot\frac{1}{g x} - \frac12 k\,\frac{x}{m g} && \text{(cancel } m \text{ in the first term, } x \text{ in the second)} \end{aligned}

Symbols as above. Units check: \frac{\mathrm{m^2/s^2}}{\mathrm{m/s^2}\cdot\mathrm m} = 1 and \frac{\mathrm{N/m}\cdot\mathrm m}{\mathrm{kg}\cdot\mathrm{m/s^2}} = \frac{\mathrm N}{\mathrm N} = 1: both terms are dimensionless, as a friction coefficient must be. Limiting case: without friction (\mu_d = 0) the equation becomes \tfrac12 m v_0^2 = \tfrac12 k x^2, all kinetic energy in the spring.

The board ends with a ratio of energies, with no derivation:

\frac{E_\text{final}}{E_\text{initial}} = 1 - \frac{4\,\mu_d\, g\, x_\text{max}}{v_0^2}
Symbols
  • E_\text{initial} = \tfrac12 m v_0^2 — kinetic energy when the block first touches the spring (J)
  • E_\text{final} — kinetic energy when the block, pushed back by the spring, passes the same point again (J) (reading explained below)
  • x_\text{max} — the maximum compression, the x above (m)
Filling the gaps

The factor 4 fits one reading: the spring pushes the block back, and E_\text{final} is its kinetic energy when it leaves the spring again. Friction has then acted over the way in and the way out, 2x_\text{max}, while the spring has returned all its stored energy:

\begin{aligned} E_\text{final} &= \tfrac12 m v_0^2 - \mu_d m g\cdot 2x_\text{max} && \text{(heat over the distance } 2x_\text{max}) \\ \frac{E_\text{final}}{E_\text{initial}} &= 1 - \frac{2\mu_d m g x_\text{max}}{\tfrac12 m v_0^2} = 1 - \frac{4\mu_d g x_\text{max}}{v_0^2} && \text{(divide by } \tfrac12 m v_0^2,\ m \text{ cancels)} \end{aligned}

(Symbols as above.) It assumes the spring force at full compression beats static friction, k x_\text{max} > \mu_s m g, otherwise the block just stays there.

Unclear (p. 1): the ratio E_\text{final}/E_\text{initial}

The board gives the formula with an arrow "⇐" and a mark below it, but no derivation and no definition of "final". The round-trip reading above (block back at the spring's relaxed end) is the only one that produces the factor 4; for the moment of maximum compression the ratio of kinetic energy lost to heat would be 2\mu_d g x/v_0^2 instead. Ask in the tutorial which was meant.

Worked example — measuring \mu_d with a spring

A 1.5 kg block hits a spring (k = 100\ \mathrm{N/m}) at v_0 = 2.0\ \mathrm{m/s} and compresses it by at most x = 0.20\ \mathrm m.

  1. Friction coefficient: \mu_d = \dfrac{(2.0)^2}{2\cdot 9.81\cdot 0.20} - \dfrac{100\cdot 0.20}{2\cdot 1.5\cdot 9.81} = 1.019 - 0.680 = 0.34.
  2. Energy book-keeping: E_\text{initial} = \tfrac12\cdot1.5\cdot2.0^2 = 3.0\ \mathrm J; spring \tfrac12\cdot100\cdot0.20^2 = 2.0\ \mathrm J; heat 0.34\cdot1.5\cdot9.81\cdot0.20 = 1.0\ \mathrm J ✓ (sums to 3.0 J).
  3. Back out: another 1.0 J of heat on the way back, so E_\text{final} = 1.0\ \mathrm J and E_\text{final}/E_\text{initial} = 1 - \frac{4\cdot0.34\cdot9.81\cdot0.20}{4} = 0.33 ✓.
  4. Does it come back? Spring force k x = 20\ \mathrm N is larger than friction \mu m g \approx 5\ \mathrm N, so yes (assuming \mu_s is not far above \mu_d).

2 Momentum conservation applied: sticking together and recoil

Lecture: p. 1 bottom – p. 2 middle, p. 11 middle · Giancoli §9-2, §9-6

The heading "Collisions & Momentum" repeats the start of 12 Energy Conservation in Practice, Momentum and Collisions › 6 Linear momentum: linear momentum \vec p = m\cdot\vec v, and Newton's second law in momentum form,

\vec F = \frac{\mathrm d}{\mathrm dt}\left(m\vec v\right) = m\cdot\frac{\mathrm d}{\mathrm dt}\vec v = m\cdot\vec a = \frac{\mathrm d}{\mathrm dt}\left(\vec p\right) \qquad (m = \text{const})
Symbols
  • \vec F — net force on the body (N); \vec p = m\vec v — its linear momentum (kg·m/s)
  • m — mass (kg), here constant ("m: konstant" on the board); \vec v, \vec a — velocity (m/s) and acceleration (m/s²)

Pulling m out of the derivative needs m constant; section 4 shows what changes when it isn't. Conservation of linear momentum (the board adds "3rd Newton axiom", because the derivation in 12 Energy Conservation in Practice, Momentum and Collisions › 7 Conservation of momentum rests on the reaction principle): before (unprimed) = after (primed),

m_1\vec v_1 + m_2\vec v_2 = m_1\vec v_1\,' + m_2\vec v_2\,'
Symbols
  • m_1, m_2 — masses of the two bodies (kg); \vec v_1, \vec v_2 — velocities before, \vec v_1\,', \vec v_2\,' — after the collision (m/s)

Board sketch: m_1 moves down-right with \vec v_1, m_2 up-right with \vec v_2; pasted figure: two balls before, during (equal and opposite forces \vec F, -\vec F) and after a collision, with their momenta.

Inelastic collision (stick together): one common final velocity \vec v_c,

m_1\vec v_1 + m_2\vec v_2 = (m_1 + m_2)\cdot\vec v_c \quad\Longrightarrow\quad \vec v_c = \frac{m_1\vec v_1 + m_2\vec v_2}{m_1 + m_2}
Symbols
  • \vec v_c — common velocity of the stuck bodies after the collision (m/s); "c" for common (it is also the velocity of the centre of mass, 3 Center of Mass)
  • m_1, m_2, \vec v_1, \vec v_2 — as above

Example: equal masses, in 2D. With m_1 = m_2 = m the mass cancels and \vec v_c is the plain average:

\vec v_c = \frac{m\vec v_1 + m\vec v_2}{2m} = \frac12\left(\vec v_1 + \vec v_2\right), \qquad \vec v_1 = \begin{pmatrix}10\\0\end{pmatrix}\mathrm{\tfrac ms},\ \ \vec v_2 = \begin{pmatrix}10\\10\end{pmatrix}\mathrm{\tfrac ms} \ \Rightarrow\ \vec v_c = \frac12\begin{pmatrix}20\\10\end{pmatrix}\mathrm{\tfrac ms} = \begin{pmatrix}10\\5\end{pmatrix}\mathrm{\tfrac ms}

Symbols as above; vectors in components (x, y). The vector equation is two equations at once, one per component: in x both move at 10 m/s, so the pair keeps 10 m/s; in y only one moves (10 m/s), so the pair gets half of it.

Unclear (p. 2): "\tfrac12(\vec v_1 + \vec v_1)"

The board writes the second term as \vec v_1 again; from the line before it and from the numbers it must be \tfrac12(\vec v_1 + \vec v_2).

Example: recoil of a rifle. Pasted figure (German): (a) "vor dem Schuss" (before the shot, "before"): rifle and bullet at rest; (b) "nach dem Schuss" (after the shot, "after"): bullet K (Kugel) flies right with v_K', momentum p_K'; rifle G (Gewehr) moves left with v_G', momentum p_G'. Given m_B = 0.05\ \mathrm{kg} (bullet), m_g = 5\ \mathrm{kg} (gun), v_B' = 120\ \mathrm{m/s}. Before the shot both are at rest, so the total momentum is zero, and stays zero:

\underbrace{m_B v_B + m_g v_g}_{0} = m_B v_B' + m_g v_g' \ \ \Rightarrow\ \ v_g' = -\frac{m_B\, v_B'}{m_g} = -\frac{0.05\ \mathrm{kg}}{5\ \mathrm{kg}}\cdot 120\ \mathrm{\tfrac ms} = -1.2\ \mathrm{\tfrac ms}
Symbols
  • m_B, m_g — masses of bullet and gun (kg); v_B, v_g — their velocities before the shot (both 0), v_B', v_g' — after (m/s), x axis in the bullet's direction
  • the minus sign: the gun moves opposite to the bullet (recoil)

The explosion's forces are internal (gas pushes bullet forward and gun back equally), so they can't change the total momentum. The gun is 100 times heavier, so it moves 100 times slower.

Example: throwing a ball from a board (p. 11). Board sketch, axes x right, y up: a person stands on a board on the floor and throws a ball to the left (arrow ←); the board with the person moves to the right (arrow →). Between board and floor "\mu \neq 0", next to it "\mu \ll". START: everything at rest, \vec p = 0. END: \vec p = -\vec p_\text{ball} + \vec p_\text{board}, the ball's momentum to the left and the board's (with the person) to the right. If the friction under the board is small (\mu \ll 1), no noticeable external force acts during the short throw, so \vec p stays (approximately) \vec 0 and the two momenta are equal and opposite: throwing something backwards pushes you forwards, the principle of every rocket.

Unclear (p. 11): the mark above \vec p at END

Above the END equation the board writes either "= 0" or "\neq 0" (a stroke runs through it). With "\mu \neq 0" both make sense: strictly, friction is an external force, so \vec p is not exactly conserved (\neq 0); with "\mu \ll" it is approximately 0. The physics is the same: the smaller the friction, the closer \vec p_\text{board} = \vec p_\text{ball}.

3 Elastic collisions in one dimension

Lecture: p. 2 bottom – p. 4 middle · Giancoli §9-5

In an elastic collision (board): the linear momentum remains constant, and the mechanical energy remains constant. On a horizontal line there is no change in height, so this means the kinetic energy is the same before and after. Two equations, so for given masses and initial velocities the two final velocities are determined. Motion is along one line (x), and the v's are x components with signs.

\text{Energy:}\quad \tfrac12 m_1 v_1^2 + \tfrac12 m_2 v_2^2 = \tfrac12 m_1 v_1'^2 + \tfrac12 m_2 v_2'^2 \qquad \text{Momentum:}\quad m_1 v_1 + m_2 v_2 = m_1 v_1' + m_2 v_2'
Symbols
  • m_1, m_2 — masses (kg); v_1, v_2 — velocities (x components) before, v_1', v_2' — after the collision (m/s), positive to the right
  • the board crosses out every \tfrac12: multiplying the energy equation by 2 removes them

Solving a quadratic system directly is messy; the lecture's trick turns it into a linear one. Collect each body's terms on one side:

\begin{aligned} m_1\,(v_1 - v_1') &= m_2\,(v_2' - v_2) && \text{I} \quad \text{(momentum: } m_1 \text{ terms left, } m_2 \text{ terms right)} \\ m_1\,(v_1^2 - v_1'^2) &= m_2\,(v_2'^2 - v_2^2) && \text{(energy, }\times 2\text{, same sorting)} \\ m_1\,(v_1 - v_1')(v_1 + v_1') &= m_2\,(v_2' - v_2)(v_2' + v_2) && \text{II} \quad (a^2 - b^2 = (a - b)(a + b)) \end{aligned}

Symbols as above. Now divide II by I. The left side of II divided by the left side of I leaves (v_1 + v_1'); the same on the right leaves (v_2' + v_2):

v_1 + v_1' = v_2' + v_2 \quad\Longrightarrow\quad v_1 - v_2 = -\left(v_1' - v_2'\right)
Symbols
  • v_1 - v_2 — velocity of body 1 relative to body 2 before the collision (m/s); v_1' - v_2' — the same after (m/s)
Filling the gaps

Dividing needs v_1 \neq v_1' (and so v_2 \neq v_2'); the case v_1' = v_1, v_2' = v_2 also solves both equations but means the bodies missed each other. The second form follows by moving terms: v_1 + v_1' = v_2' + v_2 \Rightarrow v_1 - v_2 = v_2' - v_1' = -(v_1' - v_2').

Intuition

v_1 - v_2 = -(v_1' - v_2') says: in an elastic head-on collision the bodies separate exactly as fast as they approached, whatever the masses. Seen from body 2, body 1 comes in at some speed and bounces straight back at the same speed, like a ball off a wall. This linear equation replaces the energy equation and is far easier to solve with.

Example: different masses, static target (v_2 = 0). The two equations become

m_1 v_1 = m_1 v_1' + m_2 v_2', \qquad v_1 = -\left(v_1' - v_2'\right)

and the lecture states the result:

v_1' = \frac{m_1 - m_2}{m_1 + m_2}\cdot v_1, \qquad v_2' = \frac{2 m_1}{m_1 + m_2}\cdot v_1
Symbols
  • v_1 — velocity of the incoming body 1 (m/s); body 2 is at rest before (v_2 = 0)
  • v_1', v_2' — velocities after (m/s); a negative v_1' means body 1 bounces back
  • m_1, m_2 — masses (kg)
Filling the gaps

From the second equation, v_1' = v_2' - v_1. Put this into the momentum equation:

\begin{aligned} m_1 v_1 &= m_1\,(v_2' - v_1) + m_2 v_2' && \text{(substitute } v_1') \\ 2 m_1 v_1 &= (m_1 + m_2)\, v_2' && \text{(add } m_1 v_1 \text{ to both sides, collect } v_2') \\ v_2' &= \frac{2 m_1}{m_1 + m_2}\, v_1 && \text{(divide by } m_1 + m_2) \\ v_1' &= v_2' - v_1 = \left(\frac{2 m_1}{m_1 + m_2} - \frac{m_1 + m_2}{m_1 + m_2}\right) v_1 = \frac{m_1 - m_2}{m_1 + m_2}\, v_1 && \text{(common denominator)} \end{aligned}

Symbols as above.

The lecture then reads off three limiting cases:

  • I: m_1 \gg m_2 (bowling ball hits a ping-pong ball): v_1' \approx \frac{m_1}{m_1}v_1 = v_1, \ v_2' \approx \frac{2m_1}{m_1}v_1 = 2v_1. The heavy body carries on undisturbed; the light one flies off at twice its speed.
  • II: m_2 \gg m_1 (ball against a wall): v_1' \approx \frac{-m_2}{m_2}v_1 = -v_1, \ v_2' \approx \frac{2m_1}{m_2}v_1 \approx 0\ \mathrm{m/s}. The light body bounces back with the same speed; the heavy one hardly moves.
  • III: m_1 = m_2 (billiard balls): v_1' = \frac{0\ \mathrm{kg}}{2m_1}v_1 = 0\ \mathrm{m/s}, \ v_2' = \frac{2m_1}{2m_1}v_1 = v_1. The balls swap velocities: the first stops dead, the second leaves with all the speed.

Board, p. 3: a link to a file share, https://seafile.aau.at/f/8ad2eef0a75b4e009296/ (content not stated, most likely a demonstration video).

Worked example — a light cart hits a heavier one

A 0.30 kg cart at v_1 = 4.0\ \mathrm{m/s} hits a 0.90 kg cart at rest, elastically.

  1. Formulas for a static target: v_1' = \frac{0.30 - 0.90}{1.20}\cdot 4.0 = -2.0\ \mathrm{m/s}, \ v_2' = \frac{0.60}{1.20}\cdot4.0 = 2.0\ \mathrm{m/s}.
  2. Momentum check: before 0.30\cdot4.0 = 1.2; after 0.30\cdot(-2.0) + 0.90\cdot2.0 = 1.2\ \mathrm{kg\,m/s} ✓.
  3. Energy check: before \tfrac12\cdot0.30\cdot16 = 2.4\ \mathrm J; after 0.6 + 1.8 = 2.4\ \mathrm J ✓.
  4. Relative velocity: 4.0 - 0 = -(-2.0 - 2.0) ✓. The lighter cart bounces back (m_1 < m_2 makes v_1' negative).

Example: two blocks pushed apart by a spring (p. 3 bottom – p. 4). Sketch: blocks m_1 and m_2 with a compressed spring between them, released from rest. The spring's push is internal, and both start at rest, so the total momentum stays zero:

\underbrace{m_1 v_1 + m_2 v_2}_{0} = m_1 v_1' + m_2 v_2', \qquad \text{e.g. } m_1 = \tfrac12 m_2:\quad 0 = \tfrac12 v_1' + v_2' \ \Rightarrow\ v_1' = -2\, v_2'

Symbols as above (v_1', v_2': velocities after release; the board cancels m_2). The kinetic energies:

E_1 = \frac12 m_1 v_1'^2 = \frac12\cdot\frac{m_2}{2}\left(-2v_2'\right)^2 = \frac12\cdot\frac{m_2}{2}\cdot 4 v_2'^2 = m_2\, v_2'^2, \qquad E_2 = \frac12 m_2 v_2'^2 = \frac12 E_1
Symbols
  • E_1, E_2 — kinetic energies of blocks 1 and 2 after release (J)
  • m_1 = \tfrac12 m_2 — block 1 has half the mass

The momenta are equal and opposite, but the energies are not: the lighter block gets twice the energy, \tfrac23 of what the spring stored. Since E = \frac{p^2}{2m}, equal p means the smaller mass carries more energy.

Example: two stacked balls dropped on the floor (p. 4). Sketch: a small ball 2 (m_2) sits on top of a big ball 1 (m_1 \gg m_2); the floor (m_3 \gg m_2) below. Board: v_{11} = v_{12}, v_{21} = -v_{11}, and

E_2 = \frac12 m_2\left(-3v_1\right)^2 = 9\cdot\frac12 m_2 v_1^2 = 9\,E_\text{initial}

"should go 9 times as high if perfectly elastic!"

Symbols
  • v_{ij} — read as: velocity at moment i (1 = just before ball 1 hits the floor, 2 = just after) of ball j; so v_{11} = v_{12}: both balls fall with the same velocity, v_{21} = -v_{11}: ball 1 bounces off the floor with reversed velocity
  • v_1 — the falling speed of both balls just before impact (m/s)
  • E_2 — kinetic energy of the small ball after the bounce (J); E_\text{initial} = \tfrac12 m_2 v_1^2 — its kinetic energy before (J)
Filling the gaps

Where the -3v_1 comes from, with up as positive and v_1 > 0 the falling speed: ball 1 bounces off the floor first (case II above: a light ball off a heavy "wall") and moves up at v_1, while ball 2 still moves down at v_1. They approach each other at 2v_1. Ball 1 is much heavier (case II again, now ball 2 against ball 1), so it barely changes; by "relative velocity reverses", ball 2 leaves ball 1 at 2v_1 upwards relative to ball 1, which itself moves up at v_1: ball 2 moves up at 2v_1 + v_1 = 3v_1. The board writes it as -3v_1 with v_1 the signed velocity before impact (pointing down): three times as fast, in the opposite direction. Squared, the sign doesn't matter. Height scales with v^2 (h = v^2/2g), so 9 times the kinetic energy means 9 times the drop height. Real balls lose energy at each bounce, so the small ball rises less, but still much higher than it was dropped from.

Unclear (p. 4): the index notation v_{11}, v_{12}, v_{21}

The board doesn't define the two indices. The reading above (first index = moment, second = ball) is the only one for which both board equations are true; with the other order, "v_{11} = v_{12}" would claim a ball doesn't change velocity at the floor.

Common mistake — "momentum conserved" means each body keeps its momentum

Conservation is about the total. In every example here each body's momentum changes a lot (the rifle goes from 0 to -6\ \mathrm{kg\,m/s}); only the sum stays fixed. Likewise "elastic" doesn't mean each body keeps its kinetic energy, only that the sum does.

Problem-solving steps — elastic collision in 1D
  1. Fix the x axis; give every velocity its sign.
  2. Write momentum: m_1 v_1 + m_2 v_2 = m_1 v_1' + m_2 v_2'.
  3. Instead of the energy equation, use v_1 - v_2 = -(v_1' - v_2').
  4. Solve the two linear equations (for a target at rest use v_1' = \frac{m_1 - m_2}{m_1 + m_2}v_1, v_2' = \frac{2m_1}{m_1 + m_2}v_1).
  5. Check one limiting case (m_1 = m_2: velocities swap) and that the total kinetic energy is unchanged.

4 Systems of variable mass: the conveyor belt

Lecture: p. 4 bottom – p. 5 middle ("Changing Masses") · Giancoli §9-10

\vec F = m\vec a assumed a constant mass. A conveyor belt being loaded with sand, or a rocket burning fuel, changes its mass all the time. The general law \vec F = \mathrm d\vec p/\mathrm dt still holds, but only for a fixed set of particles, so the system is chosen as the body M plus the small mass \mathrm dM that joins it during \mathrm dt.

Pasted figure: (a) a small mass \mathrm dM moving with velocity \vec u is about to join a body M moving with \vec v; (b) afterwards the combined body M + \mathrm dM moves with \vec v + \mathrm d\vec v.

Momentum after minus momentum before:

\mathrm d\vec p = \left(M + \mathrm dM\right)\left(\vec v + \mathrm d\vec v\right) - \left(M\vec v + \mathrm dM\,\vec u\right)
Symbols
  • M — mass of the main body at time t (kg); \vec v — its velocity (m/s)
  • \mathrm dM — the small mass added during \mathrm dt (kg); negative if mass leaves (rocket)
  • \vec u — velocity of \mathrm dM before it joins (m/s); \mathrm d\vec v — change of the body's velocity during \mathrm dt (m/s)
  • \mathrm d\vec p — change of the total momentum of the system M + \mathrm dM (kg·m/s)
Filling the gaps

Multiply out (the board ticks off the terms one by one):

\begin{aligned} \mathrm d\vec p &= M\vec v + M\,\mathrm d\vec v + \mathrm dM\,\vec v + \mathrm dM\,\mathrm d\vec v - M\vec v - \mathrm dM\,\vec u && \text{(expand the product)} \\ &= M\,\mathrm d\vec v + \left(\vec v - \vec u\right)\mathrm dM && (M\vec v \text{ cancels; } \mathrm dM\,\mathrm d\vec v \text{ is a product of two small quantities, dropped)} \\ \vec F_\text{ext} = \frac{\mathrm d\vec p}{\mathrm dt} &= M\,\frac{\mathrm d\vec v}{\mathrm dt} - \left(\vec u - \vec v\right)\frac{\mathrm dM}{\mathrm dt} && \text{(divide by } \mathrm dt;\ \vec v - \vec u = -(\vec u - \vec v)) \end{aligned}

Symbols as above. "Dropped": after dividing by \mathrm dt that term becomes \mathrm dM\cdot\frac{\mathrm d\vec v}{\mathrm dt}, which goes to zero with \mathrm dM.

The result, as boxed on the board:

\vec F_\text{ext} = \frac{\mathrm d\vec p}{\mathrm dt} = M\cdot\frac{\mathrm d\vec v}{\mathrm dt} - \left(\vec u - \vec v\right)\cdot\frac{\mathrm dM}{\mathrm dt}
Symbols
  • \vec F_\text{ext} — net external force on the body (N), e.g. the belt's drive
  • M\,\frac{\mathrm d\vec v}{\mathrm dt} — mass times acceleration, as usual
  • (\vec u - \vec v) — velocity of the incoming mass relative to the body (m/s); \frac{\mathrm dM}{\mathrm dt} — rate at which mass is added (kg/s), positive when mass joins
  • the second term is the "force caused by adding (or losing) mass" (board)

Example: conveyor belt. Pasted figure: sand falls vertically from a hopper onto a belt moving to the right with v. Given \dot m = \frac{\mathrm dM}{\mathrm dt} = 75\ \mathrm{kg/s}, v = 2.2\ \mathrm{m/s} (constant). What force must the belt's drive supply?

\vec F_\text{ext} = \underbrace{M\,\frac{\mathrm dv}{\mathrm dt}}_{0} - \left(u - v\right)\frac{\mathrm dM}{\mathrm dt} = -\left(0 - v\right)\frac{\mathrm dM}{\mathrm dt} = +2.2\ \mathrm{\tfrac ms}\cdot 75\ \mathrm{\tfrac{kg}s} = 165\ \mathrm N
Symbols

  • v — belt speed (m/s), constant, so \frac{\mathrm dv}{\mathrm dt} = 0

  • units: \mathrm{\tfrac ms}\cdot\mathrm{\tfrac{kg}s} = \mathrm{kg\,m/s^2} = \mathrm N ✓

The belt doesn't speed up, yet it needs a force: every second it must give 75 kg of new sand the momentum 75\cdot2.2 = 165\ \mathrm{kg\,m/s}. Required power (11 Gravitational Field, Work, Kinetic and Potential Energy › 10 Power):

P = \frac Wt = \vec F\cdot\vec v = 165\ \mathrm N\cdot 2.2\ \mathrm{\tfrac ms} = 363\ \mathrm W
Symbols

  • \vec F, \vec v — the drive force and the belt velocity, parallel here

The sand gains kinetic energy at the rate \tfrac12\dot m v^2 = \tfrac12\cdot75\cdot2.2^2 = 181.5\ \mathrm W, exactly half of 363 W. The other half is turned into heat while each grain slides on the belt until it has caught up with it (sticking is an inelastic collision). Computing the power from kinetic energy alone gives a drive that's too weak by a factor 2.

Connection

The same equation with \mathrm dM < 0 is the rocket equation: gas leaves backwards with relative velocity \vec u - \vec v, and the term (\vec u - \vec v)\,\frac{\mathrm dM}{\mathrm dt} is the thrust (Giancoli §9-10). It's the throw-the-ball-off-the-board idea of section 2, done continuously.

5 Rotation as a vector: \vec v = \vec\omega\times\vec r

Lecture: p. 5 bottom ("Rotational Motion") · Giancoli §10-1, §10-2

Pasted figures: (left) a disc on an axle rotating counter-clockwise; a point at position \vec r (from the axle) has velocity \vec v tangent to its circle, at two positions; (right, "Right-Hand-Rule") a hand around the axle: fingers curl with the rotation, the thumb points along \vec\omega, upward.

From 7 Rotational Kinematics and Circular Motion › 3 Angular velocity and angular acceleration, a point at distance r from the axis moves with speed v = \omega\cdot r. The vector form gives the direction as well:

v = \omega\cdot r, \qquad \vec v = \vec\omega\times\vec r
Symbols
  • \vec\omega — angular velocity vector (rad/s): its length is the rotation rate, its direction lies along the axis, by the right-hand rule (fingers curl with the rotation, thumb gives \vec\omega)
  • \vec r — position of the point, measured from a point on the axis (m); r — its distance from the axis (m)
  • \vec v — velocity of the point (m/s), tangent to its circle; \times — cross product (2 Vectors and Vector Products › 7 Vector product ("cross product"))
Intuition

Why put a rotation's vector along the axis? Because the axis is the only direction that doesn't change during the rotation: every point of the disc moves in a different direction, but all share the same axis and the same \omega. The cross product then rebuilds each point's velocity: perpendicular to both the axis and \vec r (tangent to the circle), with size \omega r when \vec r lies in the disc's plane.

7 Moment of inertia and rotational kinetic energy

Lecture: p. 6 – p. 7 middle ("Rotational Energy") · Giancoli §10-5, §10-8

A rotating rigid body has kinetic energy although its centre may not move: every piece moves on a circle. Split the body into small pieces m_i. Piece i circles the axis at radius r_i' (the perpendicular distance, not \lvert\vec r_i\rvert), so its speed is v_i = r_i'\cdot\omega, the same \omega for every piece because the body is rigid. Sum the kinetic energies:

\begin{aligned} E_\text{rot} &= \sum_i \tfrac12 m_i v_i^2 && \text{(kinetic energy of all pieces)} \\ &= \sum_i \tfrac12 m_i\left(r_i'\,\omega\right)^2 && (v_i = r_i'\,\omega) \\ &= \sum_i \tfrac12 m_i\, r_i'^2\,\omega^2 = \frac12\underbrace{\sum_i m_i\, r_i'^2}_{\text{moment of inertia } J}\cdot\,\omega^2 && (\omega \text{ is the same for all: out of the sum}) \end{aligned}
Symbols
  • m_i — mass of piece i (kg); r_i' — its perpendicular (shortest) distance from the rotation axis (m)
  • v_i — its speed (m/s); \omega — angular velocity of the body (rad/s)
  • E_\text{rot} — rotational kinetic energy (J); J — moment of inertia (kg·m²)
E_\text{rot} = \frac12 J\cdot\omega^2 \qquad \left(\text{compare } E_\text{kin} = \tfrac12 m v^2\right), \qquad J = \sum_i m_i\, r_i'^2, \qquad J = \int_V \rho\cdot r^2\,\mathrm dV, \qquad [J] = \mathrm{kg\,m^2}
Symbols
  • J — moment of inertia "of the object about a given axis" (board) (kg·m²); Giancoli writes I
  • \rho — density of the body (kg/m³), \mathrm dm = \rho\,\mathrm dV (3 Center of Mass › 4 Extended bodies: continuous notation)
  • r — in the integral: perpendicular distance of the volume element \mathrm dV from the axis (m), the continuous version of r_i'
  • V — the body's volume (m³); \int_V — integral over the whole body

The board also writes E_\text{rot} = \tfrac12 J\omega^2 = \tfrac12\omega^2\int_V\rho\, r^2\,\mathrm dV.

Intuition

J is the rotational version of mass: how hard a body is to set spinning. It depends not only on how much mass there is but on where it sits, and with the square of the distance from the axis: mass twice as far out counts four times. That's why a flywheel has its mass at the rim, and why "the" moment of inertia of a body doesn't exist: change the axis and J changes.

Example (p. 6–7): two masses, m_1 = 5.0\ \mathrm{kg} and m_2 = 7.0\ \mathrm{kg}, 4.0 m apart on a light rod. Figure: I — the axis is midway, r_1 = 2\ \mathrm m, r_2 = 2\ \mathrm m; II — the axis is 0.50 m to the left of m_1, r_1' = 0.5\ \mathrm m, r_2' = 4.5\ \mathrm m.

\text{I:}\ \ J = \sum_i m_i r_i'^2 = m_1 r_1^2 + m_2 r_2^2 = 5\ \mathrm{kg}\,(2\ \mathrm m)^2 + 7\ \mathrm{kg}\,(2\ \mathrm m)^2 = 48\ \mathrm{kg\,m^2}
\text{II:}\ \ J = \sum_i m_i r_i'^2 = 5\ \mathrm{kg}\,(0.5\ \mathrm m)^2 + 7\ \mathrm{kg}\,(4.5\ \mathrm m)^2 = 1.25 + 141.75 = 143\ \mathrm{kg\,m^2}
Symbols
  • r_1, r_2 (case I), r_1', r_2' (case II) — distances of the masses from the axis (m); here the prime only marks case II
  • J — moment of inertia about the respective axis (kg·m²); the rod's own mass is neglected

Same masses, same rod: three times the moment of inertia, only because the axis moved. Section 8 explains the jump with the parallel-axis theorem.

A solid steel disc, M = 20\ \mathrm{kg}, R = 0.25\ \mathrm m, spins at 300 rpm about its axis.

8 Calculating moments of inertia: hollow cylinder and parallel-axis theorem

Lecture: p. 7 bottom – p. 9 middle (13 Nov) · Giancoli §10-7

The second lecture (13.11.2026) restarts from the continuous form, J = \int r^2\,\mathrm dm (the "2" circled in red: the distance enters squared). For a body of constant density (\rho = \text{const}), m = V\cdot\rho and \mathrm dm = \mathrm dV\cdot\rho, so

J = \int r^2\,\mathrm dm = \int r^2\rho\,\mathrm dV = \rho\int r^2\,\mathrm dV
Symbols
  • r — perpendicular distance of the mass element \mathrm dm (volume element \mathrm dV) from the axis (m)
  • \rho — density, constant (kg/m³); \mathrm dm = \rho\,\mathrm dV — mass of the element (kg)

Board sketch "CENTER OF MASS": a square with axes x, y through its middle and "x_s, y_s = 0": the coordinates are placed so that the centre of mass (s = Schwerpunkt) is the origin. This is used for the parallel-axis theorem below.

Hollow cylinder. Board sketch: a ring with inner radius R_1, outer radius R_2 (the inner hole marked with a red cross: no mass there), axes x, y, height H; the rotation axis is the cylinder's symmetry axis. The trick: cut the cylinder into thin cylindrical shells of radius r and thickness \mathrm dr. Every piece of a shell has the same distance r from the axis, so the shell contributes simply r^2\,\mathrm dm. Its volume: unroll the shell into a flat slab ("ASSUMPTION" on the board: thin enough to unroll) of length = circumference 2\pi r, height H, thickness \mathrm dr.

Volumes on the board: solid cylinder V = r^2\pi\cdot H; hollow cylinder V = (R_2^2 - R_1^2)\cdot\pi\cdot H; a shell of thickness (R_2 - R_1) at radius r, approximately V = H\cdot2\pi r\cdot(\text{thickness}), so for the thin shell

\mathrm dV = H\, 2\pi r\,\mathrm dr
Symbols
  • H — height of the cylinder (m); r — radius of the shell (m), between R_1 and R_2; \mathrm dr — its thickness (m)
  • \mathrm dV — volume of the shell (m³): circumference × height × thickness

Now integrate from the inner to the outer radius:

\begin{aligned} J &= \rho\int_{R_1}^{R_2} r^2\, H\, 2\pi r\,\mathrm dr = \rho\, 2\pi H\int_{R_1}^{R_2} r^3\,\mathrm dr && \text{(constants out of the integral)} \\ &= 2\pi H\rho\left.\frac{r^4}{4}\right|_{R_1}^{R_2} = \frac{2\pi H\rho}{4}\left(R_2^4 - R_1^4\right) && \left(\textstyle\int r^3\,\mathrm dr = \frac{r^4}{4}\right) \\ &= \frac12\pi H\rho\left(R_2^2 - R_1^2\right)\left(R_2^2 + R_1^2\right) && (a^2 - b^2 = (a + b)(a - b) \text{ with } a = R_2^2,\ b = R_1^2) \\ &= \frac12\,\rho\, V\left(R_2^2 + R_1^2\right) && (\pi H (R_2^2 - R_1^2) = V,\ \text{the cylinder's volume}) \\ J &= \frac12\, m\left(R_2^2 + R_1^2\right) && (\rho V = m) \end{aligned}
Symbols
  • R_1, R_2 — inner and outer radius (m); m — mass of the hollow cylinder (kg); V — its volume (m³)
  • J — moment of inertia about the symmetry axis (kg·m²); matches table row (d)

Check with limiting cases: R_1 = 0 (solid cylinder) gives \tfrac12 m R_2^2, row (c) ✓; R_1 \to R_2 = R (thin tube, all mass at R) gives \tfrac12 m\cdot2R^2 = mR^2, the hoop of row (a) ✓. The height H dropped out: a long tube and a short ring of the same mass and radii have the same J about this axis.

Parallel-axis theorem. Board sketch: a body (hatched) with its own axes x, y, z through its centre of mass; at distance d from it a second, parallel set of axes, the "CENTER OF ROTATION". The body rotates about an axis that is parallel to one through its centre of mass, shifted by d. Every distance changes from r to r + d:

J = \int r^2\,\mathrm dm \ \Rightarrow\ J = \int (r + d)^2\,\mathrm dm = \int\left(r^2 + 2rd + d^2\right)\mathrm dm = \int r^2\,\mathrm dm + \int 2rd\,\mathrm dm + \int d^2\,\mathrm dm
Symbols
  • r — distance of \mathrm dm from the axis through the centre of mass (m); r + d — from the new axis (m)
  • d — distance between the two parallel axes (m), a constant
  • m — total mass of the body (kg)

The last term is \int d^2\,\mathrm dm = d^2\cdot m (d is constant). The middle one is crossed out in red: 2d\int r\,\mathrm dm = 0, "CENTER OF MASS". So

J_{PA} = \int r^2\,\mathrm dm + d^2 m, \qquad \boxed{\,J_{PA} = J_b + d^2\cdot m\,}
Symbols
  • J_{PA} — moment of inertia about the shifted, parallel axis (PA … parallel axis) (kg·m²)
  • J_b — the "base" inertia: moment of inertia about the parallel axis through the centre of mass (kg·m²); Giancoli: I_\text{CM}
  • d — distance between the two axes (m); m — mass of the body (kg)

Names (board): parallel-axis theorem, "Steiner's theorem", "Steiner–Huygens theorem".

Why is \int r\,\mathrm dm = 0, and why must the base axis go through the centre of mass?

The centre of mass is defined by \vec r_s = \frac1m\int\vec r\,\mathrm dm (3 Center of Mass › 4 Extended bodies: continuous notation). With the origin at the centre of mass ("x_s, y_s = 0" on the board), \int\vec r\,\mathrm dm = m\,\vec r_s = \vec 0: the mass on one side of the axis balances the mass on the other. That's what kills the cross term. If the base axis does not pass through the centre of mass, the cross term is not zero and J_b + m d^2 is wrong. So the theorem always connects the centre-of-mass axis with another axis; it never jumps directly between two off-centre axes.

Unclear (p. 8): (r + d)^2 written with scalars

The board writes distances as numbers, (r + d)^2 = r^2 + 2rd + d^2. Taken literally that is only true for pieces that lie on the line joining the two axes; for a piece elsewhere the distances don't simply add. The correct version uses vectors perpendicular to the axis: \lvert\vec r + \vec d\rvert^2 = r^2 + 2\,\vec r\cdot\vec d + d^2, and the cross term 2\,\vec d\cdot\int\vec r\,\mathrm dm vanishes by the centre-of-mass argument. The result J_{PA} = J_b + d^2 m is correct.

Changing between two off-centre axes. Board sketch: a body (hatched) with its centre of mass at the origin; one axis at distance d_1, another at distance d_2. If J_{PA} about the axis at d_1 is known, go back to J_b first, then to the axis at d_2:

J_b = J_{PA}(d_1) - d_1^2\, m, \qquad J_{PA}(d_2) = J_b + d_2^2\, m
Symbols
  • J_{PA}(d_1), J_{PA}(d_2) — moments of inertia about axes at distances d_1, d_2 from the centre of mass, all parallel (kg·m²)
  • J_b, m — as above
Worked example — the two-mass rod of section 7 with Steiner

  2. Base inertia: J_b = 5\cdot2.333^2 + 7\cdot1.667^2 = 27.22 + 19.44 = 46.67\ \mathrm{kg\,m^2}, the smallest possible for this rod.
  3. Case I (axis at 2 m, d = 0.333\ \mathrm m): J = 46.67 + 12\cdot0.333^2 = 48\ \mathrm{kg\,m^2} ✓.

Problem-solving steps — moment of inertia
  1. Point masses: J = \sum m_i r_i'^2 with distances measured perpendicular to the axis.
  2. Standard body about its centre: take J_b from the table.
  3. Axis parallel but shifted by d: J = J_b + m d^2 (only from the centre-of-mass axis).
  4. Composite body: add the J's of the parts, all about the same axis.
  5. New shape: cut it into pieces at equal distance (shells, rings, slices), write \mathrm dm = \rho\,\mathrm dV and integrate; check limiting cases.

10 Angular momentum

Lecture: p. 10 middle – p. 11 top · Giancoli §11-1, §11-3, §11-5

Following the table: linear momentum \vec p = m\cdot\vec v with \frac{\mathrm d\vec p}{\mathrm dt} = \vec F (boxed). ⇒ Angular momentum \vec L:

\vec L = \vec r\times\vec p \quad\to\quad \frac{\mathrm d\vec L}{\mathrm dt} = \vec T

Why does torque change angular momentum, \mathrm d\vec L/\mathrm dt = \vec T?

Differentiate the cross product with the product rule (the order of factors stays):

\frac{\mathrm d\vec L}{\mathrm dt} = \frac{\mathrm d\vec r}{\mathrm dt}\times\vec p + \vec r\times\frac{\mathrm d\vec p}{\mathrm dt} = \underbrace{\vec v\times m\vec v}_{\vec 0} + \vec r\times\vec F = \vec T

The first term vanishes because \vec v and m\vec v are parallel (cross product of parallel vectors is \vec 0); the second uses \mathrm d\vec p/\mathrm dt = \vec F. So torque is to angular momentum what force is to momentum.

For a rigid body rotating about an axis, summing \vec r_i\times m_i\vec v_i over all pieces gives (board, boxed)

  • L_S, L_E — angular momentum at the start and at the end (S = Start, E = Ende) (kg·m²/s)
  • r\cdot F — the torque (N·m), constant during \Delta t; \Delta t — time the force acts (s)
  • \vec p_S, \vec p_E — linear momentum at start and end (kg·m/s); \vec F — constant force (N)
  • units: \mathrm{N\,m\,s} = \mathrm{kg\,m^2/s} ✓

These are \frac{\mathrm d\vec L}{\mathrm dt} = \vec T and \frac{\mathrm d\vec p}{\mathrm dt} = \vec F for a constant torque and force: the change is rate times time. Torque × time ("angular impulse") is what changes angular momentum, just as force × time (impulse) changes momentum. For a fixed axis and constant J: \frac{\mathrm d}{\mathrm dt}(J\omega) = J\alpha = T, the rotational F = ma promised by section 9.

Unclear (p. 10): "2F" next to "Time"

Below the units the board has a mark that reads like "2F" (or "↓F", "ΔF"), with an arrow to the word "Time" that points at the \Delta t of the next line. Most likely it is a note that the force F acts over a time; it plays no role in the equations.

Worked example — spinning up a wheel

A wheel with J = 0.40\ \mathrm{kg\,m^2} is at rest; a tangential force of 20 N acts at its rim, r = 0.30\ \mathrm m, for 2.0 s.

  1. Torque: T = r F = 0.30\cdot20 = 6.0\ \mathrm{N\,m}.
  2. Angular momentum: L_E = 0 + 6.0\cdot2.0 = 12\ \mathrm{kg\,m^2/s}.
  3. Angular velocity: \omega = L_E/J = 12/0.40 = 30\ \mathrm{rad/s}.
  4. Check: \alpha = T/J = 15\ \mathrm{rad/s^2}, \omega = \alpha t = 30\ \mathrm{rad/s} ✓.

11 Conservation of angular momentum

Lecture: p. 11 top · Giancoli §11-1, §11-6

If no external torque acts, \mathrm d\vec L/\mathrm dt = \vec 0:

\Delta\vec L = 0, \qquad \vec L = \text{const} \ \ \to\ \ J\uparrow\ \omega\downarrow, \quad J\downarrow\ \omega\uparrow
Symbols
  • \Delta\vec L — change of the angular momentum of the system (kg·m²/s)
  • J — the system's moment of inertia (kg·m²), which may change (arms in or out); \omega — its angular velocity (rad/s)
  • ↑, ↓ — increases, decreases; with L = J\omega constant, one goes up when the other goes down

The skater's arms are part of the system; pulling them in is internal, and the ice exerts (almost) no torque about the vertical axis. So J_1\omega_1 = J_2\omega_2: less mass far out means a smaller J, hence a larger \omega.

Worked example — the skater

J_1 = 3.5\ \mathrm{kg\,m^2} (arms out), spinning at 2.0 rev/s; arms in: J_2 = 1.4\ \mathrm{kg\,m^2}.

  1. Conservation: \omega_2 = \frac{J_1}{J_2}\,\omega_1 = \frac{3.5}{1.4}\cdot2.0 = 5.0\ \mathrm{rev/s} (a ratio, so rev/s is fine here).
  2. Energy: \frac{E_2}{E_1} = \frac{J_2\omega_2^2}{J_1\omega_1^2} = \frac{J_1}{J_2} = 2.5.
  3. Interpretation: the kinetic energy grows by 150 %: the skater's muscles do work pulling the arms in against the "centrifugal" pull.
Common mistake — conserving the rotational energy too

L = J\omega is conserved, E_\text{rot} = \tfrac12 J\omega^2 = \frac{L^2}{2J} is not: with L fixed, a smaller J means more energy. Setting \tfrac12 J_1\omega_1^2 = \tfrac12 J_2\omega_2^2 gives \omega_2 = \omega_1\sqrt{J_1/J_2}, the wrong answer. It's the rotational version of section 2: momentum is conserved, kinetic energy generally not.

Filling the gaps

The stool turns freely about the vertical axis, so no external torque acts about it and the vertical component of the total angular momentum stays what it was: zero (at the start the wheel's \vec L is horizontal, the person at rest). After the wheel is turned upright it carries +L upwards, so person + stool must take -L: they start to rotate opposite to the wheel. Example: wheel J_w = 0.12\ \mathrm{kg\,m^2} at 40\ \mathrm{rad/s} gives L = 4.8\ \mathrm{kg\,m^2/s}; with person + stool J_p = 3.0\ \mathrm{kg\,m^2} they turn at \omega_p = 4.8/3.0 = 1.6\ \mathrm{rad/s}, about one turn every 4 s. The demonstration only works because \vec L is a vector: turning the wheel's axis changes its vertical component even though its spin rate doesn't change.

Connection

The same principle steers satellites without fuel: a reaction wheel inside is spun up one way, and the satellite turns the other way. Robot balancing and quadcopter yaw control (rotors spinning in opposite pairs, so their angular momenta cancel) rest on it too.

12 Tops and gyroscopic precession

Lecture: p. 11 bottom – p. 12 · Giancoli §11-7

The lecture closes with demonstrations: "TIPPY TOP" (German "Stehaufkreisel", written "TIPPE TOP" on the board), a top that, spun fast on its round end, flips over and keeps spinning on its stem; and an embedded video, "Gyroscopic Precession", showing a lecturer with a spinning bicycle wheel. No equations are given for either.

Intuition — precession

Hold a spinning wheel by one end of its axle only: gravity's torque about your hand points horizontally, perpendicular to \vec L. By \mathrm d\vec L = \vec T\,\mathrm dt the change of \vec L is horizontal and sideways, so the axle doesn't fall: it swings around horizontally (precession). Torque changes the direction of \vec L, not its size, just as a centripetal force changes the direction of \vec v in circular motion (7 Rotational Kinematics and Circular Motion › 4 Uniform circular motion). The faster the wheel spins (the larger L), the slower it precesses.

Beyond the lecture (Giancoli §11-7)

For a wheel of angular momentum L supported at distance r from its centre of mass, the precession rate is \Omega = \frac{M g r}{L} = \frac{M g r}{J\omega} (M: mass, \omega: spin rate). The tippe top's flip needs friction torques at its contact point and is beyond this course.
